The rolling process of this structure was consistent with that of the layered CLAM steel, but to completely recrystallize the deformed grains, the rolled steel was subjected to a solid solution treatment at 980 ◦ C for 30 min before being water quenched to room temperature to obtain a fully martensitic

The CLAM steel, with a chemical composition (in wt.%) of Fe - 8.91% Cr - 1.4% W - 0.54 % Mn - 0.15% Ta - 0.15% V- 0.09% C - 0.06% Si, was melted in a vacuum induction furnace prior to casting an ingot with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 120 mm.

The ingot was solution treated in an air furnace at 1200 ◦ C for 2 h to homogenize the microstructure and completely dissolve primary carbides, prior to hot and then warm rolling to extensively elongate the prior-austenite grains along the rolling direction.
With a starting hot rolling temperature of 1150 ◦ C, the ultimate rolling temperature was 1050 ◦ C with a deformation rate of 50%;
with the starting warm rolling temperature as 850 ◦ C, the ultimate rolling temperature was 800 ◦ C with a deformation rate of 80%.
During subsequent cooling, the austenite was completely transformed into martensite to form a laminated martensite microstructure.

To prepare the lamellar grain structure in the CLAM steel, the steel was directly tempered at 700 ◦ C for 15 min to transform the martensite into ferrite but to prevent the ferrite grains undergoing complete recrystallization.

Fig. 2 d-l shows the TEM images of the lamellar grain CLAM steel; the diffraction pattern revealed that the steel is a pure BCC ferrite structure ( Fig. 1 d). The ferrite laths had an average thickness of ~170 nm, with boundaries decorated with a short rod-like precipitate phase;

Energy spectrum analysis ( Fig. 2 f-k) and fast Fourier transform (FFT) diffractograms of a high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) image of the rod-like precipitate phase ( Fig. 2 l) revealed that it is a M 23 C 6 carbide which is rich in Cr and W ( Fig. 2 d).

In addition to the M 23 C 6 carbide, there was also a large number of MX carbides in the ferrite laths, with an average size of ~15 nm and a total volume fraction of 0.1; this is described in more details in the Supplementary Materials (Fig. S4).

attributes.morphology: lamellar along RD and TD, random along ND

evidence.quote: the lamellar steel exhibits a lamellar grain structure, in which the distributions of the grain boundaries are lamellar along the rolling (RD) and transverse (TD) directions, but random along the normal direction (ND); the average width of the lamellar grains is ~10 μ m.

In contrast, for the equiaxed grain steel, after rolling and the solid solution and tempering treatments, due to the complete recrystallization during the solid solution treatment stage, the grains exhibit a typical equiaxed structure, with an average grain size of ~10 μ m (Fig. S2 a-c).

It is apparent that after tensile fracture at room temperature, a layered tearing crack of roughly 0.3 mm appeared near the fracture surface of the lamellar grain CLAM steel for both the RD and TD orientations ( Fig. 4 a,c);
at 77K, a layered tearing crack can also be seen in both orientations but at a size increased to about 2.5 mm ( Fig. 4 b,d).

For the room temperature tensile fracture surface in the lamellar grain CLAM steel, the reduction in area (RA) is 68%;
At 77K, the RA is 25%, and the formation of these delamination tears was further promoted, such that the fracture surface was divided into two parts ( Fig. 5 d).

Similar to the tensile fracture morphology, the equiaxed CLAM steel also exhibits typical ductile fracture with a 72% reduction in area ( Fig. 5 f,g) and brittle ( Fig. 5 h,i) fracture with a 0.6% RA, respectively at room temperature and 77 K.

The superior low temperature ductility of the lamellar grained steel can be attributed to an increase in grain strength at low temperatures which promotes the propagation of layered tearing cracks; this in turn leads to a significant in-crease in the necking area of the steel, thereby compensating for the decrease in ductility.

Fig. 2 d-l shows the TEM images of the lamellar grain CLAM steel; the diffraction pattern revealed that the steel is a pure BCC ferrite structure ( Fig. 1 d). The ferrite laths had an average thickness of ~170 nm, with boundaries decorated with a short rod-like precipitate phase; this phase had an average size of ~60 nm and a total volume fraction of 0.2 (determined from its area fraction in TEM images).

Energy spectrum analysis ( Fig. 2 f-k) and fast Fourier transform (FFT) diffractograms of a high-resolution transmission electron microscope (HRTEM) image of the rod-like precipitate phase ( Fig. 2 l) revealed that it is a M 23 C 6 carbide which is rich in Cr and W ( Fig. 2 d).

It is apparent that after tensile fracture at room temperature, a layered tearing crack of roughly 0.3 mm appeared near the fracture surface of the lamellar grain CLAM steel for both the RD and TD orientations ( Fig. 4 a,c);
at 77K, a layered tearing crack can also be seen in both orientations but at a size increased to about 2.5 mm ( Fig. 4 b,d).

The superior low temperature ductility of the lamellar grained steel can be attributed to an increase in grain strength at low temperatures which promotes the propagation of layered tearing cracks; this in turn leads to a significant in-crease in the necking area of the steel, thereby compensating for the decrease in ductility.
